newsitem.title: USA: Convicted mail bomber gets Alabama death sentence.
newsitem.headline: Convicted mail bomber gets Alabama death sentence.

text.p: A man convicted of masterminding a wave of mail bombings that swept the South in 1989 was given the death penalty on Monday for the murder of a federal judge killed in the bloody campaign.

Walter Leroy Moody Jr. of Rex, Ga., was sentenced to die in Alabama's electric chair after being convicted on state murder charges in November for the slaying of 11th U.S. Circuit Judge Robert Vance of Alabama.

The 61-year-old man, who had defended himself at his trial in Jefferson County Circuit Court, stood alone in blue prison fatigues before Judge William Rhea of Etowah County but showed no emotion as the sentence was announced.

During an hour-long hearing, Moody read a rambling statement in which he told the open court that his conviction had been "fraudulent" and that Judge Rhea had been part of a wide-ranging conspiracy against him.
Moody was diagnosed in 1990 as suffering from a paranoid personality disorder and Rhea considered the diagnosis as a mitigating circumstance before opting for the death penalty.
"It is the judgment of the court that the aggravated circumstances far outweigh the mitigating circumstances," Rhea said as he imposed the sentence.
Prosecutors say Moody sent four mail bombs from August through December 1989 to targets in Alabama, Georgia and Florida.
Judge Vance died on Dec. 16, 1989, when a package he was opening in his Mountain Brook home exploded. His wife, Helen Vance, was injured by the blast.
Two days later, a similar bomb killed black civil rights attorney Robert Robinson of Savannah, Ga.
At the time of his state conviction last November, Moody already was serving a life sentence on federal charges stemming from the Vance and Robinson murders.

Bob Vance Jr., son of the slain jurist, said the death sentence was no surprise after a trial in which Moody had rejected the aid of defence counsel and treated the jury to behaviour that swung from angry outbursts to catatonic silences.
"He hung himself. He hung himself at the first trial. He hung himself at this trial," said Vance.
The judge's widow was not in court.

Moody also sent mail bombs to the Jacksonville, Fla., office of the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People and to the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Atlanta. Both those devices were intercepted and defused.
Officials said Moody selected Robinson and the NAACP as targets in order to cast suspicion on a white supremacist group, such as the Ku Klux Klan, and throw investigators off his trail.
Moody allegedly devised the mail bombing campaign because he was frustrated over his inability to get overturned a 1972 conviction for possessing a pipe bomb.
